name: Prospect of Whitby
hook: The Prospect of Whitby is a Grade II* listed pub on Wapping Wall in the East End, reputed to be one of the oldest riverside taverns in London, dating from around 1520.

facts.fact: Riverside Wapping pub usually dated to 1520; a strong fit for the heritage-by-water demo.

name: The Grapes
hook: The Grapes is a Grade II listed public house at 76 Narrow Street, Limehouse, on the north bank of the Thames; a pub has stood on the site since 1583.

facts.fact: Limehouse pub on Narrow Street with a long river-facing history and a visible place in Hilton's pub print shop.

name: The Hoop and Grapes
hook: The Hoop and Grapes at 47 Aldgate High Street is a Grade II* listed pub, probably built in the late 17th century; it is one of the very few timber-framed buildings in the City of London to survive from that period, standing just beyond where the Great Fire of London was halted in 1666.

name: The Seven Stars
hook: The Seven Stars is a Grade II listed pub at 53 Carey Street behind the Royal Courts of Justice; with 17th-century origins (its frontage bears the date 1602), it is one of the few City-fringe pubs to have survived the Great Fire of London.

name: The Tipperary
hook: The Tipperary is a Grade II listed pub at 66 Fleet Street; the building was built in about 1667, and the wood-panelled pub is widely reputed to be one of London's oldest Irish pubs.

name: The Dickens Inn
hook: The Dickens Inn at St Katharine Docks occupies an 18th-century timber-framed former warehouse; when the docks were redeveloped in the 1970s the structure was moved bodily to its present site and reopened as a three-storey balconied inn.

name: The Nellie Dean
hook: The Nellie Dean of Soho is a Grade II listed pub at 89 Dean Street, Soho; the present building dates from 1900 and there has been a pub on the site since the 18th century.

facts.fact: The Nellie Dean of Soho is a Grade II listed pub at 89 Dean Street, Soho; the present building dates from 1900 and there has been a pub on the site since the 18th century.

name: The Perseverance
hook: The Perseverance at 63 Lamb's Conduit Street, Bloomsbury, is a Grade II listed building of early-18th-century origin, refronted in the early 19th century; it traded for years as The Sun before taking its current name.

name: The Captain Kidd
hook: The Captain Kidd at 108 Wapping High Street is a Grade II listed riverside pub in a converted former warehouse, named after the pirate William Kidd, who was hanged at the nearby Execution Dock in 1701.

facts.fact: The Captain Kidd at 108 Wapping High Street is a Grade II listed riverside pub in a converted former warehouse, named after the pirate William Kidd, who was hanged at the nearby Execution Dock in 1701.

name: The Crown & Two Chairmen
hook: The Crown & Two Chairmen at 31-32 Dean Street, Soho, has had a pub on the site since 1736; the present building was rebuilt in 1929 and the name is said to recall two sedan-chair men who drank here while Queen Anne sat for a portrait opposite.

name: The Cheshire Cheese
hook: The Cheshire Cheese at 48 Crutched Friars sits beneath the viaduct of Fenchurch Street station in the City of London; a pub of this name traded on the site before the railway arrived in the 1850s, with records of the Cheshire Cheese, Crutched Friars going back to the early 19th century. (It is a separate pub from the famous Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese on Fleet Street.)

name: The Pride of Spitalfields
hook: The Pride of Spitalfields at 3 Heneage Street, just off Brick Lane in the East End, is a mid-19th-century pub formerly known as the Romford Arms; it sits in the old Huguenot heartland of Spitalfields and was named CAMRA's East London Pub of the Year in 2013.

name: The Star Tavern
hook: The Star Tavern is a Grade II listed pub at 6 Belgrave Mews West, Belgravia, of early-to-mid-19th-century origin; in the 1950s and 1960s it drew both high society and the London underworld, and it is reputed to be where the 1963 Great Train Robbery was planned.

name: The Bulls Head
hook: The Bull's Head at 373 Lonsdale Road, Barnes, is a riverside Young's pub whose present building dates from 1846; it opened as a jazz venue in 1959 and, hosting leading British and international musicians, became known as the 'suburban Ronnie Scott's'.

name: The Queens Arms
hook: Pimlico pub from 1846; a useful Victorian reference stop for the seeded heritage route.

name: The Rugby Tavern
hook: The Rugby Tavern on the corner of Great James Street and Rugby Street, Bloomsbury, is a Grade II listed pub dating from about 1850, built on land that forms part of the Rugby (School) Estate.

name: Museum Tavern
hook: The Museum Tavern is a Grade II listed pub at 49 Great Russell Street, opposite the British Museum; the present building was rebuilt around 1855-64 by William Finch Hill, and Karl Marx is traditionally said to have drunk here while working in the nearby Reading Room.

name: The Blackfriar
hook: The Black Friar is a Grade II* listed pub at 174 Queen Victoria Street, Blackfriars, built about 1875 on the site of a medieval Dominican (Black Friars) friary and remodelled around 1905 by the architect Herbert Fuller-Clark; it is famous for its Arts and Crafts and Art Nouveau interior of marble, mosaic and bronze reliefs of jovial friars.

facts.fact: The Black Friar is a Grade II* listed pub at 174 Queen Victoria Street, Blackfriars, built about 1875 on the site of a medieval Dominican (Black Friars) friary and remodelled around 1905 by the architect Herbert Fuller-Clark; it is famous for its Arts and Crafts and Art Nouveau interior of marble, mosaic and bronze reliefs of jovial friars.

The Black Friar was nearly lost to redevelopment in the 1960s and was saved by a preservation campaign associated with the poet Sir John Betjeman; its interior is on CAMRA's National Inventory of historic pub interiors.

name: The Old Bank of England
hook: The Old Bank of England is a Grade II listed pub at 194 Fleet Street, built in 1886 by Sir Arthur Blomfield; it housed the Law Courts branch of the Bank of England from 1888 to 1975 before becoming a pub in 1994.

name: The Audley
hook: The Audley at 41-43 Mount Street, Mayfair, is a Grade II listed pub built about 1888 to designs by the architect Thomas Verity; a grand late-Victorian building of red brick and pink terracotta, it was rebuilt on the Grosvenor (Duke of Westminster) estate and retains fine mahogany panelling and a carved bar-back.

name: The Dog & Duck
hook: The Dog and Duck at 18 Bateman Street, Soho, is a Grade II listed pub; the current building dates from 1897 and its upstairs dining room is named after the writer George Orwell, who was a regular.

name: Salisbury
hook: The Salisbury at 90 St Martin's Lane, Covent Garden, is a Grade II listed pub built about 1899; its lavish late-Victorian interior of etched and polished glass, mahogany and Art Nouveau candelabra is listed on CAMRA's National Inventory as a historic pub interior of national importance.

name: Ye Olde Watling
hook: Ye Olde Watling stands at 29 Watling Street, on the line of the old Roman road of the same name, close to St Paul's Cathedral; the timber-framed pub is traditionally said to have been rebuilt for Sir Christopher Wren's workmen after the Great Fire of London, and its present old-world interior largely dates from a sympathetic refit of about 1901.

hook: The Coal Hole is a Grade II listed pub at 91 Strand, part of the Savoy Court development, built in 1903-04 to the design of architect T. E. Collcutt.

name: The Lyceum Tavern
hook: The Lyceum Tavern at 354 Strand takes its name from the neighbouring Lyceum Theatre; a tavern has stood on the site since the 1840s and the present building dates from 1906. It is a Grade II listed pub.

name: The Old Pack Horse
hook: The Old Pack Horse is a Grade II listed pub on Chiswick High Road, rebuilt in 1910 in an Edwardian style for the Isleworth Brewery.

name: The Dolphin Tavern
hook: The Dolphin Tavern at 44 Red Lion Street, Holborn, was badly damaged by a Zeppelin raid on 8 September 1915; the pub's clock, recovered from the rubble, is preserved stopped at 10.40pm, the moment of the blast.

name: Ye Olde Cock Tavern
hook: Ye Olde Cock Tavern is a Grade II listed pub at 22 Fleet Street, listed in 1977; the tavern was moved across the street and rebuilt in the 1880s, and is traditionally said to have been frequented by Samuel Pepys, Charles Dickens and Alfred Tennyson.

hook: The Coach and Horses at 29 Greek Street, Soho, is a Grade II listed pub long associated with Private Eye magazine and with journalist Jeffrey Bernard, whose 'Low Life' column and the play 'Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell' immortalised it.

name: The Dove
hook: The Dove is a Grade II* listed pub on Upper Mall, Hammersmith, overlooking the Thames; it holds a Guinness World Record for the smallest bar room in a public house.

name: The Grenadier
hook: The Grenadier is a Grade II listed pub tucked down Wilton Row in Belgravia, taking its name from the Grenadier Guards; it is traditionally said to have served as an officers' mess and to have been frequented by the Duke of Wellington, and is well known as one of London's most famously haunted pubs.
